title: The Strange Story of Lysol
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck trace the history of Lysol, the disinfectant brand. They explain how disinfectants work at the cellular level (quaternary ammonium compounds, or quats, and alcohol combined), noting contact time matters. Lysol was invented in 1889 by German chemist Gustav Rappenstrunk (spelled as the hosts say it, "Gustav Roppenstrouk" was a mishearing; the hosts settle on the spelling used in their discussion), originally a cresol-based product sold to medical professionals, then criticized by the AMA in 1912. Lysol was remarketed for home use and as a douche and contraceptive, a practice that was widely used through the 1930s-1960s despite being dangerous and ineffective, and ended when the birth control pill arrived. Later history covers formula changes, the FTC, COVID-19 pandemic sales boom, CDC endorsement, the hygiene hypothesis and old friends hypothesis linking over-disinfecting to autoimmune disease, debate over chronic low-level exposure and ingredient disclosure legislation, far-UV germicidal light, and a listener mail segment from a physician fan.
topics: AMA Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry

segments.title: Opening and listener suggestion
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, a listener suggestion from Holland about the history of Lysol, and thank writer Kyle Hookstra.

segments.title: Lysol's market and purpose of disinfecting
segments.summary: Lysol is described as a leading disinfectant brand, with sales spiking during the COVID-19 pandemic. The hosts explain why people disinfect surfaces and that the episode is not a takedown.

segments.title: How disinfectants work
segments.summary: Disinfectants disrupt microbes' outer layers. Lysol's quats (quaternary ammonium compounds, including benzalkonium chloride) combined with alcohol denature proteins and cells. Concentration and contact time matter, and wipes often need minutes to work.

segments.title: Origins of Lysol and early medical use
segments.summary: Lysol was invented in 1889 by German chemist Gustav Rappenstrunk, originally a cresol-and-soap product for medical professionals, used for cleaning wounds. The name's etymology is uncertain. Cresol was less poisonous than carbolic acid but still caustic.

segments.title: 1912 AMA criticism and repositioning for home use
segments.summary: The AMA Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry in 1912 raised concerns about burns from Lysol. Lynn and Fink, the makers, shifted marketing to home use and to women's reproductive health.
topics: AMA Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry

segments.title: Lysol as a contraceptive douche
segments.summary: Lysol was marketed as a feminine hygiene douche and effectively became the most common US contraceptive from the 1930s through the 1960s, though illegal contraceptive marketing forced coded language. The hosts note douching kills beneficial vaginal bacteria, creating the problems it claimed to solve.

segments.title: Lysol contraceptive ads and dangers
segments.summary: Historian Kristen Hall's review of ads showed exploitative messages about marriage and sex. A 1933 study found about half of 507 women using Lysol as a douche became pregnant. Doctors Sarah Greenberg and Rachel Lynn Palmer criticized it, and the product caused injuries, poisonings, and was used in illegal abortions.

segments.title: Decline of Lysol as contraceptive
segments.summary: Use of Lysol as a contraceptive ended in the 1960s, around when the birth control pill became legal and widespread, rather than because of safety warnings.

segments.title: Formula changes and FTC pressure
segments.summary: After the 1960s, Lysol spray and other products expanded. Makers changed formulas, such as replacing cresol with ortho hydroxy phenol in 1952, to reduce toxicity amid FTC rules on truthful claims.

segments.title: COVID-19 boom and CDC recommendation
segments.summary: Disinfectant sales surged during COVID-19, with Lysol's sales up about 12 percent and reports of poisonings. Lysol's quat formula was tested by the CDC and recommended for killing the virus, boosting sales.

segments.title: Hygiene hypothesis and old friends hypothesis
segments.summary: The hosts discuss over-disinfecting possibly harming immune development. Autoimmune and allergy rates are higher in the West, and Graham Rook's old friends hypothesis argues for exposure to diverse microbes. A Finnish, Estonian, and Russian stool-sample study is cited. Chuck shares anecdotal family experience.

segments.title: Chronic exposure concerns and ingredient disclosure bill
segments.summary: Disinfectants are toxic depending on concentration, with concentrates more dangerous than ready-to-use spray. Chronic low-level exposure is understudied. Indiana Representative Larry Bucshon's federal bill would preempt California's ingredient-disclosure law; Lysol's maker supports it while Clorox opposes it.

segments.title: Far-UV germicidal light and alcohol-water disinfection
segments.summary: Far-UV germicidal light can kill airborne germs without penetrating skin or eyes, but can create ozone. Alcohol with water is more effective against viruses than alcohol alone.

segments.title: Personal germ habits
segments.summary: Hosts discuss their personal hygiene habits, including hand sanitizer versus soap and paper towels in restrooms and gas stations, and reflect on germophobia after COVID-19.

segments.title: Listener mail from Adam
segments.summary: A physician listener named Adam thanks the hosts, describing how the show accompanied him through school, residency, and driving to hospitals. The hosts respond warmly and sign off with the show's credits.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits noting Stuff You Should Know is a production of iHeartRadio.
